title: Prepare feed and feed cows in milk

lessons.title: What a cow in milk needs to eat
lessons.html:
Feeding drives the milk tank

A cow in milk turns feed into milk. If she eats less, she gives less milk, loses body condition and is slower to get back in calf. As a dairy supervisor you make sure every cow gets the right feed, in the right amount, at the right time, every day.

The main parts of the ration

  • Roughage – pasture (kikuyu, ryegrass, clover), silage, lucerne hay or oat hay. It keeps the rumen working and gives the fibre needed for milk fat.
  • Concentrates – dairy meal or pellets made from maize, soya, cottonseed oilcake and other ingredients. They give energy and protein for high yields.
  • Minerals and vitamins – usually in the meal or as a lick. Cows need calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, salt and trace elements.
  • Water – milk is mostly water. A high-yielding cow drinks a large volume every day, more in hot weather. No water means no milk.

Stage of lactation matters

Cows are fed differently through the lactation:

StageWhat to watch
Fresh cows (first weeks after calving)Appetite is low but milk rises fast. Build up concentrates slowly and give the best roughage.
Peak and mid lactationHighest intake. Feed to yield and keep feed in front of cows.
Late lactationYield drops. Avoid overfeeding so cows do not get too fat before drying off.
Dry cowsSeparate ration set by the nutritionist to prepare for calving.

Who decides the ration?

The farm manager and the animal nutritionist decide the ration. Your job is to follow the feed sheet exactly, measure feed correctly and report problems. Never change a ration on your own. Sudden changes upset the rumen and can cause acidosis, bloat or a drop in milk.

Watch the cows. Healthy cows have full left flanks, chew the cud when resting and have dung that is not too runny and not too stiff. If many cows have runny dung or are not eating, tell the manager the same day.

lessons.title: Preparing and mixing feed safely
lessons.html:
Getting the feed ready

Good feed can be spoiled by poor handling. Follow the feed sheet and these steps every time.

Before you start

  1. Check the feed sheet for each group: fresh cows, high yielders, low yielders and so on.
  2. Check that the scale on the mixer wagon or the meal bins is working. Weigh, do not guess.
  3. Look at the feed. Throw out mouldy silage, wet or caked meal and anything that smells bad. Mouldy feed can contain toxins that harm cows and can pass into milk.
  4. Keep the silage face clean. Take silage off evenly across the face and cover the rest tightly to keep air out.

Mixing a TMR

Many farms mix a total mixed ration (TMR) in a mixer wagon. Load ingredients in the order on the feed sheet, usually hay first, then silage, then concentrates and minerals. Mix for the time given. Overmixing chops the fibre too fine; undermixing lets cows sort out the meal and leave the roughage.

Machinery and feed store safety

  • Only trained and authorised workers may drive the tractor and mixer wagon.
  • Never climb into a mixer wagon or reach into augers while the power take-off (PTO) is engaged. Switch off, remove the key and wait for all parts to stop.
  • Keep PTO guards in place. Do not wear loose clothing near moving shafts.
  • Silage faces can collapse. Do not stand close under a high face.
  • Wear a dust mask when handling dusty meal and gloves when handling minerals.
  • Store feed off the floor, dry and away from rats, and keep chemicals and fertiliser away from feed.

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to provide safe machinery and training, and requires workers to follow safety rules and report hazards. If a guard is missing or a machine is faulty, stop and report it.

Record what you mixed and fed on the feed record: date, group, ingredients and kilograms. This helps the manager check costs and link feeding to milk yield.

lessons.title: Feeding cows and checking the results
lessons.html:
Putting feed in front of cows

Cows eat most when fresh feed is available after milking. Feed at the same times every day so the cows get into a routine.

Good feeding practice

  • Clean the feed trough or feed lane before putting down new feed. Remove old, hot or mouldy leftovers.
  • Spread feed evenly along the trough so shy and young cows also get a fair share.
  • Push feed up several times a day so cows can reach it.
  • Make sure there is enough trough space for all cows in the group.
  • Check water troughs daily. Clean them, check floats and make sure water flows fast enough.

Feeding in the parlour

On many farms meal is fed in the parlour by an automatic feeder set per cow or per group. Check that the feeders deliver the correct amount and that no feeder is blocked. Report any cow that does not finish her meal.

Feeding on pasture

For pasture-based herds, move cows to a fresh camp or strip as planned by the manager. Move the electric fence correctly and make sure each camp has water. Do not let hungry cows onto lush clover or ryegrass too fast, as this can cause bloat; follow the farm's bloat control plan.

Check the results

  • Refusals: weigh or estimate what is left in the trough. A small amount left means the cows had enough. An empty, licked trough means they may need more; a lot left means a problem.
  • Milk yield: a sudden drop for a group can point to a feed problem.
  • Body condition: cows that are getting very thin or very fat need the ration checked.
  • Dung and cud chewing: signs of rumen health.

Report sick cows, bloat, lame cows that cannot reach feed and any feed shortage to the manager immediately.

Key points

  • Follow the feed sheet exactly and never change a ration on your own.
  • Weigh feed and throw out mouldy or spoiled feed.
  • Switch off and remove the key before working on a mixer wagon or auger.
  • Keep troughs clean, feed available and water flowing.
  • Check refusals, milk yield and cow condition, and report problems the same day.

quiz.question: Who decides the ration for cows in milk?

options.text: The farm manager and animal nutritionist

quiz.question: What should you do with mouldy silage?

options.text: Throw it out and not feed it
Add extra meal to hide it

quiz.question: What must you do before reaching into a mixer wagon?

options.text: Ask someone to watch the PTO
Switch off, remove the key and wait for all parts to stop

quiz.question: What can happen if a ration is changed suddenly?

options.text: The rumen is upset and cows can get acidosis or bloat

quiz.question: Which part of the ration mainly gives fibre for rumen health and milk fat?

options.text: Roughage such as silage, hay or pasture
